Operator:
Good day and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the StellarTech Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a Q&A session. Today's call is being recorded.
I would now like to hand the call over to Janet Smith, Investor Relations Director. Please go ahead.

Janet Smith, Investor Relations Director:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and welcome to StellarTech’s earnings call. Joining me today are Alex Johnson, CEO; Ben Carter, CFO; and Emily Davis, Chief Technology Officer.
Earlier today, we published our earnings press release and slides, which are available on our IR site. Please note this call may contain forward-looking statements. Now, I’ll turn it over to Alex Johnson.

Alex Johnson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thanks, Janet. Hello, everyone.

Let’s start with a look at the quarter:

This quarter, we achieved significant progress, including revenue of KRW 63.7 trillion. This represents a slight sequential decline of approximately 2.5% compared to Q1 2024's KRW 65.3 trillion, but a robust year-over-year increase of 20.2% compared to Q2 2023's KRW 53.0 trillion. We navigated macroeconomic headwinds and specific challenges in the mobile sector, but strong performance in Memory, TVs, and Digital Appliances fueled overall growth. The revenue result slightly underperformed the internal guidance provided last quarter.

We’re seeing strong performance in wafer sales, and for DRAM, our bit growth reached 13%, situated in the low-teen percentage range, driven primarily by increased demand from the data center and high-performance computing (HPC) sectors. ASP for DRAM increased by 18%, positioning it in the high-teens percentage range, reflecting both strong demand and successful execution of our strategy to prioritize higher-value, specialty DRAM products.

These results reflect our strategy in action. I’ll now hand it over to Ben Carter to discuss the financials.

Ben Carter, Chief Financial Officer:
Thanks, Alex, and hello, everyone.

Let’s take a closer look at the numbers:

As Alex mentioned, for DRAM, our bit growth reached 13%, with ASP increasing by 18%. We shipped approximately 1.12 million DRAM wafers in Q2, a 7% increase compared to Q1 2024 and a 10% increase year-over-year. This growth was fueled by hyperscale data centers continuing to invest heavily in server infrastructure, particularly DDR5 memory, to support AI/ML workloads. Our DDR5 wafer shipments increased by 28% quarter-over-quarter, representing a significant portion of our total DRAM wafer output. While still below pre-pandemic levels, the PC market showed signs of stabilization in Q2, with increased demand for higher-capacity DRAM modules in both desktops and laptops. This resulted in a 5% QoQ increase in our LPDDR5 wafer shipments. We saw strong demand across all major regions, with sales in the Asia-Pacific region (excluding China) increasing by 15% QoQ, driven by the expansion of cloud infrastructure and increased smartphone production in Southeast Asia. The 18% ASP increase for DRAM reflects a favorable market dynamic and our strategic focus on value-added products. DDR5 modules commanded a significant price premium over DDR4 due to their superior performance and limited supply, and we successfully capitalized on this premium, increasing our DDR5 ASP by 12% QoQ. Our efforts to develop and market specialty DRAM products, such as high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for AI accelerators and automotive-grade DRAM for autonomous vehicles, yielded positive results. HBM sales accounted for 8% of our total DRAM revenue in Q2, with an ASP significantly higher than standard DRAM. The ongoing transition to our 1alpha node process technology also contributed to ASP growth. While the initial ramp-up involved higher costs, the increased density and performance of 1alpha DRAM allowed us to offer higher-capacity modules at a premium price. We also had favorable contract negotiations with key customers, particularly in the data center segment, securing higher prices in exchange for guaranteed supply and priority access to our latest DRAM technologies.

For sales performance by segment, the Mobile business experienced a sequential sales decline. Q3 revenue totaled $18.7 billion, a decrease of 7% compared to Q2's $20.1 billion. This decline was primarily driven by a persistent component supply shortage, particularly impacting high-end processor availability by approximately 12%, and COVID-19-related production disruptions, most notably affecting our Vietnam manufacturing facilities which saw a 20% reduction in output for a three-week period in July. These challenges were exacerbated by typical Q3 seasonality, where demand for smartphones traditionally softens ahead of the holiday season. North American sales remained relatively stable, showing a slight 2% increase year-over-year, driven by strong sales of our Galaxy Z Fold and Flip series. However, European sales declined by 10% due to macroeconomic headwinds and inflationary pressures impacting consumer spending. Asia-Pacific sales experienced the most significant decline, falling by 15%, largely due to the aforementioned production disruptions in Vietnam and increased competition from local manufacturers. While smartphone sales were down, tablets and wearables continued to contribute positively to the overall Mobile segment performance. Tablet revenue increased by 8% year-over-year, driven by the popularity of our Galaxy Tab S8 series, particularly the Ultra model, which saw a 25% increase in sales volume. Wearables, including our Galaxy Watch 5 and Buds Pro 2, also performed well, with a 15% increase in Q3 revenue year-over-year to $2.3 billion. Despite the sales decline, we successfully maintained solid profitability in the Mobile segment. Our operating margin remained robust at 14.5%, a slight decrease from Q2's 15%, but still within our target range. This was achieved through proactive supply chain management, diversifying our component sourcing and negotiating favorable pricing agreements. We also saw significant improvements in our cost structure through streamlining our manufacturing processes and optimizing our marketing spend.

Now to Emily, who will cover operational and product updates.

Emily Davis, Chief Technology Officer:
Thanks, Ben.

Let’s revisit our revenue results from an innovation standpoint:
The sequential decline of approximately 2.5% in total revenue compared to Q1 was primarily due to a contraction in the Mobile eXperience (MX) business, specifically smartphone sales. The second quarter is traditionally a period of softer demand following the launch of flagship devices in Q1. Furthermore, the MX division faced exacerbated component supply shortages, particularly for key display drivers and certain high-end camera sensors. This shortage impacted production volumes, hindering the company's ability to fully meet existing demand for its Galaxy S24 series and newer foldable devices. We estimate that the component shortages alone accounted for a 1.8% drag on overall revenue. However, the substantial year-over-year growth of 20.2% was driven by strong performances across several key divisions. The Memory division saw a remarkable recovery, contributing significantly to the overall YoY increase. Revenue from memory chips jumped by an estimated 35% compared to Q2 2023. This growth was fueled by surging demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI accelerators and data centers, as well as a rebound in DRAM and NAND flash prices due to improved market dynamics and inventory normalization across the industry. Specifically, HBM3 sales increased by 60% YoY. The TV business demonstrated resilience, with revenue increasing by approximately 12% YoY, supported by strong sales of premium TVs, including Neo QLED 8K and OLED models. Furthermore, our strategic focus on larger screen sizes (75 inches and above) proved successful, with sales of these models increasing by 25% YoY. The Digital Appliances division continued its growth trajectory, reporting an increase of approximately 18% YoY, driven by strong demand for premium appliances, including Bespoke refrigerators and AI-enabled washing machines, particularly in North America and Europe. Expansion into emerging markets, such as India and Southeast Asia, also contributed to this growth.

We launched the StellarX chip which contributed to NAND experiencing a more moderate but still positive performance in Q2. Bit growth reached 8%, sitting in the high single-digit percentage range, primarily driven by demand from the mobile and enterprise SSD markets. ASP for NAND increased by 6%, remaining in the mid-single digit range, reflecting a more competitive pricing environment compared to DRAM. We shipped approximately 950,000 NAND wafers in Q2, a 4% increase compared to Q1 2024 and a 7% increase YoY. This growth was driven by increased demand for high-capacity NAND flash in smartphones, particularly in the premium segment. The adoption of 512GB and 1TB storage options in flagship devices contributed significantly to our growth. Demand for enterprise SSDs remained strong, driven by the continued growth of cloud computing and the increasing adoption of NVMe SSDs in data centers. While pricing remained competitive, we saw increased demand for our higher-density, 176-layer NAND products. The client SSD market experienced a slight rebound in Q2, driven by increased PC sales and the adoption of SSDs as standard storage in laptops. We saw increased demand for our lower-capacity, value-oriented SSDs. The 6% ASP increase for NAND reflects a more competitive pricing environment but also our strategic focus on high-value applications. The ongoing transition to our 176-layer NAND technology allowed us to offer higher-density products at a competitive price, contributing to overall ASP growth. While the cost per bit decreased, the increased capacity per wafer led to higher ASPs. We continued to focus on differentiating our enterprise SSD offerings through advanced features such as enhanced data security, improved endurance, and optimized performance for specific workloads, allowing us to command a premium over commodity NAND flash. We are focusing on increasing the number of layers and cells in our 3D NAND to increase capacity and performance while reducing the overall cost per bit. ASPs varied across regions. In North America and Europe, we were able to maintain higher ASPs due to strong demand from enterprise customers. In Asia-Pacific, pricing remained more competitive due to increased competition from local NAND manufacturers.

We’ve made strong headway with addressing supply chain vulnerabilities, and expect meaningful results in Q3. Addressing these vulnerabilities is a top priority. We are actively working to diversify our component sourcing and strengthen relationships with key suppliers. Furthermore, the company needs to closely monitor the competitive landscape and differentiate its products through innovative features and designs. The upcoming launch of the Galaxy Z Fold 6 and Z Flip 6 in Q3 is expected to drive revenue growth in the MX division.

Let’s move to Q&A.

Q&A SESSION

Analyst 1:
On wafer sales, could you expand on NAND's performance and future strategies?

Ben Carter:
Absolutely. We believe that moving forward, we will continue to focus on process technology leadership by investing heavily in R&D to maintain our leadership in DRAM and NAND process technology. Our next-generation 1gamma node for DRAM and 232-layer NAND technology are expected to enter production in late 2024 or early 2025, further enhancing our cost competitiveness and performance. We will continue to diversify our product portfolio by developing specialty DRAM and NAND solutions for emerging applications such as AI, automotive, and edge computing. Supply chain optimization will also be key, ensuring a stable supply of wafers and materials, mitigating the impact of potential disruptions. Finally, we will explore opportunities to expand our presence in emerging markets, particularly in Southeast Asia and India, to capitalize on the growing demand for memory products.

Analyst 2:
Regarding sales guidance, what's the scale and outlook for Q3 and the full year?

Emily Davis:
We’re seeing momentum with our Q3 and full-year guidance, reflecting a cautiously optimistic outlook, tempered by macroeconomic uncertainties and evolving market dynamics within the memory, display panel, and consumer electronics sectors. While we anticipate aligning with market growth rates in DRAM and NAND, challenges in the display panel segment and shifting consumer preferences require proactive adjustments to our strategy. We are focused on optimizing our product mix, enhancing operational efficiencies, and strategically investing in key growth areas, particularly in advanced NAND technologies and high-end OLED displays.
For DRAM, we project market bit growth to be in the low single-digit range (approximately 2-4%). Our own DRAM bit growth is expected to closely mirror the market, landing us at roughly 3%. This translates to an estimated DRAM revenue of $7.8 billion for Q3, representing a slight increase of 1% quarter-over-quarter. While overall bit growth is modest, we anticipate a positive ASP (Average Selling Price) impact due to a higher proportion of DDR5 sales, which command a premium. We expect DDR5 to account for 65% of our DRAM revenue in Q3, up from 58% in Q2. Our outlook for the full year remains positive, with an expectation of mid-20% market bit growth in DRAM (approximately 25%). We anticipate matching this growth rate, resulting in a full-year DRAM revenue target of $31.5 billion, representing a 22% increase year-over-year.
For NAND, we expect market bit growth in the low teens (approximately 12-14%). We forecast our NAND bit growth to align with the market, positioning us for approximately 13% bit growth in Q3. This translates to an estimated NAND revenue of $5.5 billion, reflecting a 10% increase quarter-over-quarter. We expect the NAND market to grow by approximately 40% for the full year, and we are targeting a similar growth rate. We are targeting a full-year NAND revenue of $21 billion, representing a 38% increase year-over-year.

Closing

Alex Johnson:
Thank you all for joining. We’re proud of our progress and excited for what’s ahead.

Operator:
Thank you. This concludes the call. You may now disconnect.
